newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain approves 1997 budget seen assuring EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: Spain approves 1997 budget seen assuring EMU goal.

text.p: Spain's parliament approved the 1997 budget on Friday with higher public expenditures than initially proposed but the government said it was still firmly on course to qualify European Monetary Union from the start.
Markets welcomed the confirmation with stocks setting record highs on Friday and bonds gaining as well despite subdued holiday trade.
"(The budget) guarantees Spain's entrance into the Monetary Union with its rigour and austerity," Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said after parliament gave the budget a green light.
The 1997 budget slashes total spending to just 1.7 percent by cutting or freezing outlays in all sectors expect pensions, health and regional transfers.
Rato acknowledged public expenditures will be higher than originally forecast, increasing the total deficit by 11.27 billion pesetas.
The budget was approved with 200 amendments to the initial draft which will increase total public expenditures by 0.0157 percent of Spain's GDP, Rato explained in a news conference.

Lopez Amor, parliamentary spokesman for the ruling Popular Party called the new budget "very credible" and said the increase in expenditures would not hinder the government's goal of keeping total public deficit to around 3.0 percent of GDP.
That is the level which the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria set out as a key yardstick for 1997, the year countries will be judged to qualify for a single currency set to be launched in 1999.
In a vote of confidence in the budget, first unveiled in September, markets have been rallying for months.
"From my point of view the budget approval is a confirmation that the Spanish outlook will remain positive," said Graham McDevitt economist at Paribas Capital markets in London.
"We expect a sell-off in all bonds markets the first quarter next year, but we recomand to buy Spain on weakness," he added.
The bond market was subdued due to year-end holidays but was the only one to gain in Europe on Friday.
At 1530 GMT, the long-term future contract was trading at 112.15, up 37 basis points from Thursday and near its all-time high of 112.40.

"I thought everything about the budget was already discounted. But since bonos are the only one to gain, I have to admit the approval is considered as positive," said an economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The 10-year spread over German Bunds was trading at around 110 basis points. It was at 330 in March when the Popular party was elected and at around 500 basis points in the summer of 1995.
At the same time the stock market was setting new highs, registering a 40 percent gain for the year, the best performer in the world outside emerging markets.
With 1997 inflation expected around 2.6 percent and growth seen at three percent, the government hopes now to boost employment, a crucial issue in the country.
The budget law was approved by Popular Party, the Catalan Convergency and Union party, the Canary Coalition and the moderate Basque National Party.
